prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(after the Russian) The piano has crawled into the quarry. Hauled In last night for firewood, sprawled With frozen barrels, crates and sticks, The piano is waiting for the axe. Legless, a black box, still polished; It lies on its belly like a lizard, Droning, heaving, hardly fashioned For the quarry’s primordial art. Blood red: his frozen fingers cleft, Two on the right hand, five on the left, He goes down on his knees to reach the keyboard, To strike the lizard’s chord. Seven fingers pick out rhymes and rhythm, The frozen skin, steaming, peels off them, As from a boiled potato. Their schemes, Their beauty, ivory and anthracite, Flicker and flash like the great Northern Lights. Everything played before is a great lie. The reflections of flaming chandeliers— Deceit, the white columns, the grand tiers In warm concert halls—wild lies. But the steel of the piano howls in me, I lie in the quarry and I am deft As the lizard. I accept the gift. I’ll be a song for Russia, I’ll be an étude, warmth and bread for everybody.

(after the Russian)

The piano has crawled into the quarry.  
Hauled in last night for firewood, sprawled  
with frozen barrels, crates, and sticks,  
the piano is waiting for the axe.  
Legless, a black box, still polished,  
it lies on its belly like a lizard,  
droning, heaving, hardly fashioned  
for the quarry’s primordial art.

two on the right hand, five on the left—  
he goes down on his knees to reach the keyboard,  
to strike the lizard’s chord.

the frozen skin, steaming, peels from them

their beauty, ivory and anthracite,  
flicker and flash like the great Northern Lights.

Everything played before is a great lie.  
The reflections of flaming chandeliers—  
deceit; the white columns, the grand tiers  
in warm concert halls—wild lies.  
But the steel of the piano howls in me.  
I lie in the quarry, and I am deft  
as the lizard. I accept the gift.  
I’ll be a song for Russia;  
I’ll be an étude, warmth, and bread for everybody.
outputs.L2:
After the Russian:

The piano has made its way down into the quarry.  
Dragged there the previous night to be chopped for fuel,  
it lies among frozen barrels, boxes, and pieces of wood,  
waiting for the blade.

Without legs, a glossy black case,  
it rests flat on its underside like a lizard,  
humming and straining, scarcely suited  
to the quarry’s ancient craft.

Blood-red, his frostbitten fingers are split—  
two on the right hand, five on the left.  
He lowers himself to his knees to reach the keys,  
to sound the lizard’s note.

With seven fingers he searches out meter and rhyme.  
The frozen skin steams and strips away  
like the peel of a boiled potato.  
Their patterns, their loveliness—ivory and coal-black—  
spark and flare like the vast aurora borealis.

All music performed before this was a magnificent falsehood.  
The glow of blazing chandeliers reflected back—  
a fraud; the white pillars, the sweeping balconies  
of heated concert halls—extravagant untruths.

But the piano’s steel cries out inside me.  
I am lying in the quarry, quick and skillful  
as the lizard. I receive the offering.  
I will become a song for Russia;  
I will become an étude, heat and bread for everyone.
outputs.L3:
In the quarry lies a discarded piano, abandoned and stripped of every trace of its former elegance. Once perhaps an instrument of refinement, polished rooms, and cultivated applause, it now rests among stone and cold earth, reduced almost to scrap. Its beauty has been taken from it; its purpose seems over. It waits not for a musician, but for an axe — to be chopped apart for firewood, to become fuel rather than song.

Yet into this bleak scene comes a figure who kneels before the ruined instrument. His fingers are frozen, wounded, and stiff with cold, but still he reaches toward the keys. The act is painful and almost impossible, but he plays. In that brutal landscape, where the piano no longer belongs to the world of comfort or artifice, the music begins again. It is not graceful in the conventional sense, nor is it meant to charm.

The sound that rises from the quarry rejects the polished beauty of concert halls. It has nothing to do with velvet curtains, bright chandeliers, or audiences trained to admire what is elegant and safe. This music refuses deception. It does not pretend that suffering is beautiful, nor does it hide hardship beneath refinement. Instead, it comes from ruin, cold, hunger, and endurance.

Because of this, the piano’s raw sound becomes more powerful than any carefully perfected performance. Its broken music speaks with the force of truth. It carries suffering, but also resilience: the determination to create warmth where there is none, to make meaning from what has been discarded, and to turn pain into expression. The wounded hands do not merely play notes; they testify to survival.

The speaker receives this harsh music not as something ugly, but as a gift. It is a song born from deprivation, yet it offers sustenance. It is firewood transformed back into music, cold transformed into warmth, despair transformed into hope. In its roughness, the speaker hears a deeper beauty — a beauty honest enough to belong to Russia itself. This music becomes a prayer, a nourishment, and a promise that even in ruin, life and truth can still sing.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the image of a discarded piano abandoned in a freezing quarry, transforming a broken musical instrument into the center of a harsh and visionary landscape. Instead of placing music in a refined concert hall, surrounded by elegance, comfort, and cultivated listeners, the poem situates it among stone, cold, hunger, and bodily exhaustion. The piano is no longer a polished object of art; it is exposed, damaged, and almost corpse-like. Yet this ruin does not silence it. On the contrary, the bleak setting intensifies its meaning, making the instrument seem both wounded and alive.

Through stark and surreal imagery, the poem connects artistic creation with physical suffering. The frozen quarry becomes a place where the boundaries between object and body, music and pain, beauty and deprivation begin to blur. The piano appears not merely as an instrument but as a victim of history and hardship, something that has endured violence and neglect. Its brokenness mirrors the suffering of people who live through poverty, cold, and labor. At the same time, the possibility of music remains present within it, suggesting that art can survive even in conditions that seem designed to destroy it.

The poem therefore rejects the idea that true music belongs only to wealth, refinement, or cultural privilege. It suggests that music born from comfort may be less profound than music wrested from suffering. In the quarry, amid deprivation, music becomes more than entertainment or ornament. It becomes a form of nourishment, a means of survival, and a sign of human solidarity. The piano’s imagined music speaks for those who endure hardship and transforms their suffering into a shared spiritual resource.

In this way, the poem presents art as a gift created through endurance. Music is not separated from hunger, cold, labor, or national suffering; it arises from them and answers them. For Russia, as the poem imagines it, art becomes a kind of sustenance, something that helps people continue living when material comfort is absent. The ruined piano in the frozen quarry thus becomes a powerful symbol: out of abandonment and pain comes a music that is deeper, more communal, and more necessary than anything produced in ease.
outputs.L5:
**The Russian Hauled Across the Snow**

The Russian winter had settled over the village like a heavy white blanket. Roads disappeared beneath deep snow, and even the tallest pines bent under the weight of ice. At dawn, the old horse was harnessed to a wooden sled, and the villagers gathered near the frozen river.

The sled was hauled slowly across the snow, carrying sacks of grain, firewood, and letters from distant towns. Every creak of the runners echoed in the cold air. The Russian landscape seemed endless—silent fields, dark forests, and a pale sky stretching far beyond the horizon.

Though the journey was difficult, it was necessary. In that harsh season, everything depended on patience, strength, and the steady rhythm of those who hauled what others needed to survive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an English poem “after the Russian” in which a broken piano in a quarry becomes a symbol of art, suffering, and revolutionary Russia.
counterfactuals.output:
**Broken Piano in the Quarry**  
*after the Russian*

In the quarry, where frost gnaws the stone,  
a piano lies open like a blackened mouth.  
No house remembers it. No child  
practices scales in the yellow afternoon.  

Its legs are splintered. Its wires, exposed,  
glitter like nerves in the workers’ dawn.  
When the wind passes through them, it plays  
not music, but iron, hunger, snow.  

Comrades with hammers descend the pit,  
their coats stiff with dust and history.  
They do not touch the keys. They know  
what songs have cost the human hand.  

Once, perhaps, it stood in a room  
where officers danced and candles wept,  
where a girl in white learned Chopin  
while peasants froze beyond the glass.  

Now red flags climb the winter air.  
The old world cracks like shale underfoot.  
Still, from the ruined instrument,  
a dark chord trembles through the earth.  

O Russia—wounded mother, factory, field—  
you drag your music through blood and stone.  
You break the piano, yet keep the sound;  
you bury art, and hear it rise.  

At evening, the quarry fills with blue.  
The workers lift their faces, listening.  
Somewhere beneath the shattered keys  
the future strikes its first note.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stark, imagistic free-verse translation/adaptation of a Soviet-era Russian poem featuring a pianist with frozen fingers playing a discarded piano for warmth and bread.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t provide a translation/adaptation of an unspecified Soviet-era poem that may still be under copyright, but here is an original free-verse poem built from the premise and imagery you described:

---

**Piano for Heat**

In the courtyard  
behind the canteen,  
snow fills the throat  
of a black piano.

Someone has dragged it there  
like a horse  
too old for the front.

Its lid hangs open.  
Its strings are ribs.  
The pedals are three cold tongues  
licked mute by frost.

A pianist sits before it  
on an upturned crate,  
hands wrapped in rags,  
fingers white as boiled roots.

He plays.

Not music at first—  
only knocks,  
splinters,  
the teeth of winter  
striking back.

Then a scale rises  
thin and blue  
through the apartment blocks.

Windows bloom with faces.

A woman stops  
with two empty pails.  
A soldier laughs once  
and coughs blood into his sleeve.  
Children come close enough  
to see the man’s fingers  
crack open at the nails.

He plays faster.

For heat.

For the small loaf  
waiting in somebody’s coat.  
For steam remembered.  
For a room with a stove  
and a mother turning potatoes  
in blackened hands.

The piano answers  
with its broken mouth.

Chopin loses an eye.  
Mozart limps.  
A folk song crawls out  
from under the keys  
and lies down in the snow.

The crowd listens  
as if listening could burn.

When he finishes,  
no one claps.

Clapping is waste.  
Clapping lets the cold in.

A boy steps forward  
and places bread  
on the warped music stand—  
dark bread,  
hard as a brick,  
holy as fire.

The pianist bows  
to the bread,  
to the piano,  
to the gray sky  
that has not fallen yet.

Then he breaks off a corner,  
puts it in his mouth,  
and plays again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of a Russian avant-garde translation, with images of firewood, a piano, a quarry, severed/frozen fingers, concert halls as lies, and a final pledge to be a song for Russia.
counterfactuals.output:
**I Will Be a Song**

Firewood sleeps in the yard—  
black ribs under snow,  
each log a mute soldier  
with a splintered tongue of flame.

The piano is dragged through the quarry,  
its teeth full of limestone,  
its lid flapping like a crow’s wing  
over the blue pit of morning.

Who plays?  
Not I—  
my fingers were severed by winter,  
then frozen back to the hand  
like pale little candles  
that will not burn.

The concert halls are lies.  
Gold balconies—lies.  
Velvet throats—lies.  
Applause, that soft police—lies.  
The chandeliers hang there  
like captured suns  
forced to confess.

Better the quarry’s open mouth.  
Better the firewood’s cracked psalm.  
Better the piano, wheezing in mud,  
struck by a fist of frost  
until music comes out crooked,  
barefoot, bleeding snow.

O Russia—  
vast stove of sorrow,  
field of iron lullabies,  
mother with smoke in her hair—  
take my broken keys,  
take my frozen fingers,  
take this splintered heart.

I pledge:  
I will not be marble,  
nor velvet,  
nor the lie of a hall.

I will be a song for Russia—  
rough as firewood,  
deep as a quarry,  
burning with hands  
that cannot feel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an English poetic rendering, labeled “(after the Russian),” of a bleak Russian poem where a legless black piano lies like a lizard and music becomes survival for everyone.
counterfactuals.output:
**(after the Russian)**

In the yard, the black piano lay  
legless, flat against the snow,  
like a lizard stunned by winter,  
its lacquer split, its wires exposed.

No one asked who dragged it there.  
The houses stared with broken eyes.  
Smoke unraveled from the chimneys.  
Bread was counted. Names were not.

Then someone struck a key—  
a cracked, astonished sound,  
thin as a match in the dark,  
but it burned.

And people came: the old woman  
with her shawl of rain,  
the boy with hunger in his sleeves,  
the soldier carrying silence  
like a second rifle.

They stood around that ruined beast  
as if around a stove,  
warming their hands on music  
no one owned.

What did it play? Not hope—  
hope was too expensive.  
Not joy—joy had been evacuated.  
Only the stubborn human note  
that says: we are still here,

we have not yet become snow,  
or ash, or numbers in a book.  
Strike again. Strike harder.  
Let the dead strings answer.

And the black piano, belly to earth,  
gave them what it could:  
a little thunder, a little breath,  
a road through the freezing air—

and for that hour, for everyone,  
music was not beauty.  
Music was bread.  
Music was fire.  
Music was living.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
